title: Relics shared
hookLine: the passing, the cremation, and the relics divided among eight peoples

cards: After a funeral, families sometimes fight over the strangest things. Not always the house. Sometimes a watch, a teapot, a box of letters.
Anything that still feels like the person. When the Buddha dies at Kusinara, the same thing nearly happens on the scale of kingdoms.
Seven peoples send messengers to the Mallas of Kusinara, each saying: he was one of us, too. We want a share of his remains. Tempers rise.
And the one who stops a war is not a king, and not a monk.

teach.b: First, the passing itself. After his question met silence three times, the Buddha speaks his last words to the monks: all conditioned things are subject to decay; strive on with heedfulness.

Then he moves through the meditative absorptions, up and back down and up again, and passes away. The earth shakes. Some monks weep; others, the text says, bear it mindfully: everything put together comes apart.
The Mallas honor the body for six days with music, dance and garlands.
On the seventh they carry it to the pyre, but it won't catch fire until the elder Mahakassapa arrives with his monks and bows at the Buddha's feet. Then the pyre lights.

teach.h: SEVEN PEOPLES ASK FOR A SHARE.
teach.b: Afterward, the bones remain. And the messengers come: King Ajatasattu, the Licchavis of Vesali, the Sakyans, the Bulis, the Koliyas, a brahmin of Vethadipa, the Mallas of Pava. The Mallas of Kusinara refuse: he died here.
Then a brahmin named Dona speaks up. Our teacher, he reminds them, taught patience. It isn't right to fight over the remains of the best of men.
Let's divide them into eight equal parts, so that shrines rise everywhere and many come to trust.
Everyone agrees. Dona divides the relics, and asks only for the urn. The Moriyas arrive late and take the embers.
Ten shrines rise, and the remains of the man who taught letting go are scattered, peacefully, across the land, and no one goes to war.

how: Buddhists across Asia honor relics of the Buddha and of great teachers in stupas and pagodas, walking around them clockwise, offering flowers and lights, and sitting nearby in meditation.

o: the Buddha's robe and bowl given to heirs
the remains divided so no one went to war
relics sold to fund the first monasteries

p: came late and took the embers

s: the pyre lit as soon as the Mallas tried
it would not catch until Mahakassapa arrived and bowed.
Dona kept the urn for himself
he asked for the vessel the relics had been measured in.
there were exactly eight shrines in the end
eight shares of relics, plus Dona's urn and the Moriyas' embers: ten in all.

games.q: you're Dona. seven peoples and the Mallas are about to fight over the Buddha's remains. what do you say?
o: give them all to the most powerful king.
remind them he taught patience, and divide the relics into eight shares.
bury them where no one can find them.
games.why: Dona says it isn't right to fight over the remains of one who taught patience, and divides them fairly.

practice: Today, a sit in silence: no image, no phrase, the way the monks sat after the earth stopped shaking. If a thought comes, let it pass like a messenger who arrived late, and return to the breath.
If you have time, stay a little longer, up to five minutes, just as quietly.

wordCard.voice: Relics shared. After the Buddha's passing and cremation, the brahmin Dona divides the remains among eight peoples so no one goes to war over them. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali dhatu: element, and also a relic. the word for the remains Dona shared.

carryVoice: Your line: strive on. Things come apart, so keep going, with care. That's day five hundred fifty-two.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 16 (Mahaparinibbana Sutta), the last words, the passing, the cremation and the division of relics
